R01-E-01: The case for monitoring employees at work usually rests on two claims. The first is that the employer is paying for the worker's time and is therefore entitled to know how that time is spent. The second is that the worker has agreed to the arrangement: the monitoring policy was set out in the contract, and nobody was forced to sign it. Both claims sound reasonable, and both, I think, prove much less than their defenders suppose. Take the argument from payment first. An employer buys a worker's labour, not the worker; the wage secures a certain kind of effort over a certain period, and it has never been understood to include a right to observe everything a person does while that effort is being given. A firm that pays a carpenter by the day may inspect the cabinets she builds, but it does not thereby acquire a claim to read her letters during lunch. The argument from consent fares little better. Agreement given by someone who needs the job, in a market where most comparable employers impose similar terms, tells us that the terms were accepted, not that they were fair. Consent of this kind can settle a dispute about what was agreed; it cannot settle whether the agreement should have been offered. The deeper difficulty is what continuous monitoring does to work itself. When every keystroke and pause is recorded, the employee learns to perform for the record rather than for the task. A support worker whose calls are timed will cut short a conversation with a confused customer even when a longer one would solve the problem; an office worker whose idle minutes are logged will keep the screen busy instead of stopping to think. The record begins to replace the judgement it was supposed to check, and the trust on which most skilled work depends, the expectation that a person will use discretion well when no one is looking, quietly erodes. There is an irony here as well: the information that monitoring yields grows less useful the more thoroughly it is collected, because what it captures is increasingly a display staged for the watcher. None of this means that employers may never watch. Where a job carries a specific and serious risk, such as handling cash, operating dangerous machinery or opening confidential records, targeted checks are a reasonable response to that risk, and most employees understand them as such. The test I would propose is therefore not whether monitoring was agreed to, but whether it is tied to an identifiable hazard and limited to what that hazard requires. General surveillance, justified only by the employer's wish to know, fails that test, however clearly it has been written into the contract.
R01-E-02: Many people who would never tell a lie are perfectly comfortable misleading. Asked whether he has finished a report, an employee replies that he has been working on it all morning, which is true, and which he says precisely so that his manager will conclude that the report is nearly done. He has not lied, he tells himself; if his manager draws the wrong conclusion, that is her inference, not his assertion. The intuition behind this self-defence is widely shared, and it is not merely self-serving. Ordinary moral thinking, many legal systems and a long tradition of moral reasoning have treated the outright falsehood as a graver matter than the true statement artfully deployed. Yet when we ask what is wrong with lying in the first place, the distinction begins to look thin. The harm of a lie consists chiefly in two things: the listener ends up with a false belief that he did not choose, and the trust he extended to the speaker has been turned against him. Both harms are present in the case of the employee. His manager now believes something false about the report, and she believes it because she assumed, reasonably, that a colleague answering her question was trying to answer it. The employee exploited exactly that assumption. That he did so by selecting true words rather than inventing false ones changes the technique, not the result. There is, however, one setting in which the distinction earns its keep. In a negotiation over the price of a used car, both parties know that the other is pursuing its own advantage, and each is expected to read the other's statements with suspicion. A seller who says that several people have asked about the car, when several have indeed asked but none has made an offer, leaves the buyer free to discount the remark, and a competent buyer will. Where the listener is on guard by convention, the responsibility for drawing inferences is genuinely shared, and the misleader has exploited much less trust than the liar, who asserts something false that even a wary listener has no means of checking. What this suggests is that the moral line runs less between lying and misleading than between relationships in which listeners are entitled to rely on a speaker's cooperation and those in which they are not. In the first kind, which includes most of our dealings with doctors, colleagues, friends and family, the careful choice of true but misleading words offers almost no moral shelter. In the second, it offers some. The employee who congratulates himself on never having lied has simply mistaken the setting he is in.
R01-E-03: When a patient can no longer decide for herself, someone else must decide for her, and the question is on what basis. The answer favoured in much of modern medical ethics is that the surrogate, usually a close relative, should choose as the patient would have chosen had she been able to. This standard of substituted judgement has an obvious appeal. It extends the patient's autonomy beyond the point at which she can exercise it, so that even when she is unconscious, her values rather than anyone else's continue to govern what is done to her body. The older alternative, that the surrogate should simply choose whatever is in the patient's best interests, looks paternalistic by comparison, since it invites others to put their idea of a good outcome in place of hers. The appeal is real, but it depends on there being something for the surrogate to reconstruct. Sometimes there is. A patient who said repeatedly, while healthy, that she would never want to be kept alive on a ventilator has left a clear instruction, and a daughter who honours it is doing exactly what the standard asks. Far more often, however, the situation that arises is one the patient never considered. She may have had firm views about dying at home but none about a trial of dialysis that offers a modest chance of recovery and a large chance of prolonged discomfort. To ask what she would have chosen here is to ask a counterfactual question to which there may be no fact of the matter. The surrogate who answers it confidently is not discovering the patient's will; he is extrapolating from scraps, and the extrapolation is shaped, inevitably, by his own hopes and fears. This would matter less if the fiction were harmless, but it has two costs. The first is that it hides the surrogate's own judgement behind the patient's name, so that a decision which ought to be open to discussion, with doctors and with other relatives, is presented as beyond discussion: this is simply what she would have wanted. The second is subtler. Families often find substituted judgement consoling precisely because it seems to relieve them of responsibility, and that consolation is not to be despised. But a consolation bought by pretending is fragile, and relatives who later doubt that they read the patient correctly may suffer more than they would have if they had been told, from the start, that they were being asked to judge what was best for her. The remedy is not to abandon substituted judgement but to confine it to cases where the patient's own wishes are actually known and actually bear on the decision, and to say plainly, in all other cases, that the surrogate is choosing on the patient's behalf what seems best for her. Honesty about which standard is in play is itself a form of respect for the patient.
R01-E-04: Few practices attract scorn as readily as offsetting. A traveller who pays a fee to have trees planted in compensation for the emissions of her flight is compared, almost by reflex, to the sinner who once bought a pardon: she has not stopped doing the harmful thing, the critic says, she has merely paid to feel better about it. A sharper version of the objection imagines a man who wishes to be unfaithful to his wife and pays a friend to remain faithful to his own, so that the total quantity of fidelity in the world is unchanged. If that arrangement is absurd, and it plainly is, why should paying for trees be any different? The comparison is instructive, but not in the way the critic intends. Infidelity wrongs a particular person, and the wrong consists in what is done to her; another couple's faithfulness does nothing to repair it, because she was never interested in the global supply of fidelity. The harm of greenhouse emissions has an entirely different structure. It does not fall on anyone in particular by virtue of a relationship with the emitter; it arises from the total concentration of gases in the atmosphere, to which every tonne contributes equally regardless of where it came from. A tonne removed in one place cancels a tonne added in another as far as the eventual damage is concerned. Where a harm is aggregate and interchangeable in this way, compensation elsewhere is not a moral sleight of hand. It is, at least in principle, a genuine undoing. What the fidelity case shows, then, is that offsetting is incoherent for directed wrongs and coherent for aggregate ones. One cannot offset an insult to a colleague by being kind to a stranger, but one can offset a contribution to a shared stock of harm by subtracting an equal amount from it. The serious questions about carbon offsetting are therefore not philosophical but practical: whether the trees would have been planted anyway, whether they will survive long enough to hold the carbon they are credited with, whether the accounts of the scheme can be trusted. An offset that fails these tests is not a pardon; it is simply a fraud, and the right response to it is an audit, not moral disdain. I do not want to claim that nothing remains of the critic's unease. A person who comes to regard every harm as purchasable may lose the habit of asking whether she should be doing the harmful thing at all, and a culture of easy offsetting may slow the changes in conduct that will ultimately be needed. These are real worries. But they concern the character of the offsetter and the politics of reform, not the question of whether the harm itself has been undone, and they should not be dressed up as proof that offsetting is a confidence trick.
R01-E-05: Arguments about charity tend to divide into two camps. On one side are those who hold that money given to help others should go wherever it will do the most good, which, given the vast differences in what a sum can buy in different places, often means far from home. On the other are those who insist that we owe something special to our own: our town, our region, our country. The first camp accuses the second of parochialism dressed up as loyalty; the second accuses the first of a cold arithmetic that would dissolve every bond that makes moral life recognisable. Each has hold of something, and each, I think, misidentifies what it is. Begin with what the defenders of local giving get right. There really are special obligations. A parent owes more to her own children than to children in general, and no plausible ethics of giving asks her to fund a stranger's schooling before her son's. We also owe more to those we have harmed, and to those with whom we share institutions that we sustain and from which we benefit, such as a school we attended or a cooperative to which we belong. These obligations do not arise from distance. They arise from relationships: from dependence, from history, from reciprocity. The trouble is that the case for local giving usually trades on these relationships while asking for something else. The resident who prefers to give to a shelter in his own city rather than to a health programme abroad rarely stands in any special relation to the people in the shelter. He has not harmed them, does not depend on them and shares no institution with them beyond the accident of living within the same municipal boundary. What draws him is proximity, and proximity by itself has little moral force. A sick stranger in the next street does not matter more than a sick stranger in another country simply because she is closer, though I may be better placed to help her. That last qualification points to the strongest argument for local giving, which is not about loyalty at all but about knowledge. Near home, donors can see whether their money is used well, and can withdraw it if it is not. This is a serious consideration, but it is an empirical one, and it cuts in both directions: where reliable assessments of distant programmes exist, the advantage of proximity shrinks, and where the local charity is opaque, it disappears. What remains, once relationships and knowledge are set aside, is often a preference for help whose results one can watch, a preference that is understandable but that should not be mistaken for an obligation.
R01-E-06: Whether insects can suffer is a question on which serious people disagree, and on which the evidence is likely to remain inconclusive for a long time. Their nervous systems are tiny and organised very differently from ours; some of their behaviour looks like nothing more than reflex, while some looks uncomfortably like the behaviour that, in a dog or a bird, we would take without hesitation as a sign of pain. Faced with this uncertainty, the usual response is to treat it as permission. If we cannot know that insects feel anything, the thought runs, we need not worry about how we treat them. This inference is much weaker than it looks. Uncertainty about whether a being can suffer is not the same as confidence that it cannot, and in other contexts we do not treat it so. A builder who is unsure whether a house is occupied does not demolish it on the grounds that no one has proved anyone is inside. What uncertainty calls for is a weighing: the probability that harm is occurring, multiplied by how bad the harm would be and by how many beings it would affect. With insects, the last factor is overwhelming. The numbers involved in agriculture, pest control and the growing industry that farms insects for animal feed run to many billions, so that even a modest probability of sentience yields a large expected total of suffering. The obvious objection is that this style of reasoning proves too much. If any probability of suffering above zero, multiplied by a sufficiently large number of beings, can generate an overriding moral demand, then we might find ourselves obliged to reorganise our lives around bacteria, or around the remote chance that plants feel pain. That objection has force against arguments resting on probabilities so small that they amount to mere logical possibility. It has much less force here. The case for insect sentience is not a bare possibility of the kind that could be raised for any organism; it rests on specific behavioural and physiological features that insects share with animals whose capacity for pain we already accept, even if they share them only partially. What follows is not that insects should be accorded the same consideration as mammals, nor that every crushed ant is a tragedy. It is that where we deliberately bring insects into existence in vast numbers and kill them, as in insect farming, we should prefer methods of rearing and killing that would minimise suffering if suffering is present, provided the cost of doing so is modest. Precautions of this kind ask little of us. To refuse them on the grounds that sentience has not been proved is to mistake the absence of certainty for the presence of a licence.
R01-E-07: Any decision whose costs and benefits are spread over time requires some way of comparing what happens now with what happens later, and the standard device is the discount rate. A benefit expected in a year is counted as worth somewhat less than the same benefit today; one expected in ten years, less again; and so on, at a compounding rate. Within a single human life, and over horizons of a few decades, the practice is largely uncontroversial. Its consequences become startling only when the horizon stretches across centuries. At a rate of five per cent a year, a harm that will occur two hundred years from now is valued today at a tiny fraction of one per cent of its full size, so that a policy which spared our descendants a catastrophe would barely register against even modest present costs. Whether we owe the future anything substantial thus turns, in practice, on a number that is usually set by technical convention. It helps to separate the reasons that have been given for discounting, because they do not stand or fall together. One is pure time preference: the view that well-being simply matters less the later it occurs. Another appeals to growth. If future people will be considerably richer than we are, then a given sum of money, or a given quantity of goods, will make less difference to their lives than it would to ours, much as a rupee means less to a wealthy person than to a poor one. A third appeals to uncertainty: the further away an outcome, the less sure we can be that it will happen at all, or that there will be anyone for it to happen to. Pure time preference is the weakest of these, at least when it is applied across generations. A person who prefers a pleasure today to a larger one next year may be imprudent, but the impatience is his own and so are its costs. To discount the well-being of people not yet born merely because they will be born later is a different matter: it is to treat a position in time as a reason for counting someone's suffering as less, in just the way that it would be indefensible to count suffering as less because it occurs in a distant country. The growth argument is more respectable, because it does not deny the equal standing of future people; it says only that the same resources will do them less good. But it is respectable only on its own assumptions. It presupposes that the future will in fact be richer, which is precisely what is in doubt if the harm in question is severe enough to undermine prosperity, and it applies only to losses for which wealth can compensate. A flooded coastline or an extinct species is not made good by a larger economy, and to discount such losses at the rate at which consumption grows is to treat them as though they could be bought back. The argument from uncertainty deserves more sympathy than critics of discounting usually allow it. It is reasonable to give some weight to the possibility that there will be no future people at all, and a small discount for that possibility is defensible. But the rate this argument supports is far lower than the rates commonly used, and it has nothing to say about harms we are confident will occur. What emerges from these distinctions is that the choice of a discount rate is not the technical matter it is often taken to be. Each component encodes a substantive view: about whether time itself diminishes moral standing, about how confident we are in continued growth, about which losses money can repair. A rate presented as a neutral parameter is, in effect, a verdict on what the present owes to the future, reached without the argument such a verdict requires.
R01-E-08: When a child falls into a disused well or a group of miners is trapped underground, communities will spend almost without limit to bring them out. Engineers are flown in, machines are diverted from other work, and no one asks whether the money might have been better used. The same communities, meanwhile, routinely decline measures that would save far more lives at far lower cost: safer road junctions, better lighting on rural highways, routine screening for common diseases. To many economists and policy analysts, the contrast is simply an error. A life saved by a guardrail is no less a life than one saved by a rescue shaft; that we cannot name the person in advance makes no difference to the value of what is saved. On this view the preference for identified over statistical lives is a bias, and a costly one, to be corrected by accounting that treats every life saved alike. Much of this critique seems to me correct. The people whose deaths a guardrail prevents are not abstractions; they are as real as the trapped miners, and they would have suffered and been mourned in the same way. If we spend a hundred times more per life on rescue than on prevention, a great many people die who need not have, and the fact that we never learn their names does not make their deaths any less our doing. It is worth noticing, too, that the identified lives we rush to save are often identified by chance: they are the victims whose plight happens to be reported, while others in similar danger elsewhere receive nothing, because no one is watching. Yet the critique moves too quickly when it concludes that the impulse to rescue has no rational content. What a community expresses when it refuses to abandon a known person in peril is a commitment that has value beyond the life in question: an assurance, to everyone, that if they are ever in that position they will not be left to die because the arithmetic was unfavourable. This assurance is a real good, and it is one that statistical accounting, which counts only lives saved, has no column for. It is enjoyed by people who are never in danger, and it shapes how the members of a community regard one another. Nor need this good conflict with the analyst's preferred standpoint. The strongest case for prevention is made from the position of someone who does not yet know whether he will be a victim: from there, each of us would prefer the policy that most improves our own chances, and that is usually prevention. But someone in that position would also want the assurance that rescue provides, and would be willing to pay something for it. Properly understood, then, the choice made under that uncertainty is not between rescue and prevention but about the proportion in which to buy them, and it is hard to believe that the proportion would resemble our present spending, in which prevention is starved while rescue is limitless. The lesson is not that rescue should be abandoned in the name of consistency, a policy that would purchase a few more statistical lives at the price of a community in which no one could count on being saved. It is that the scandal lies on the other side of the ledger. We do not rescue too much; we prevent too little, and the impulse to rescue, rightly valued, gives no excuse for that neglect.
